records.label: Neonatal onset PKD patient
quotes: This study reports for the first time a patient with neonatal onset of PKD homozygous for an incomplete penetrant PKD2 missense variant due to uniparental disomy.

notes.statement: Khonsari et al. (2013) deleted Pkd2 in neural crest-derived cells of mice using Wnt1Cre. The mutants showed signs of mechanical trauma, including fractured molar roots, distorted incisors, alveolar bone loss and compressed temporomandibular joints, as well as abnormal skull shapes. None of these phenotypes was seen at embryonic stages, when the head receives no significant mechanical stress in utero. The authors suggested that Pkd2 is likely to play a critical role in craniofacial growth as a mechanoreceptor.
quotes: analysed mice with conditional deletion of Pkd2 in neural crest-derived cells, using Wnt1Cre mice. Pkd2 mutants showed many signs of mechanical trauma such as fractured molar roots, distorted incisors, alveolar bone loss and compressed temporomandibular joints, in addition to abnormal skull shapes.

Significantly, mutants showed no indication of any of these phenotypes at embryonic stages when heads perceive no significant mechanical stress in utero. The results suggest that Pkd2 is likely to play a critical role in craniofacial growth as a mechanoreceptor.

notes.statement: Khonsari et al. (2013) analysed the faces of ADPKD patients with 3-dimensional photography and dense surface modelling. They found specific facial characteristics in the patients, some of which correlated with those of Pkd2 conditional mutant mice.
quotes: Since facial anomalies have never been identified in ADPKD patients, we carried out three-dimensional photography of patient faces and analysed these using dense surface modelling. This analysis revealed specific characteristics of ADPKD patient faces, some of which correlated with those of the mutant mice.

notes.statement: Khonsari et al. (2013) found that Pkd2 was expressed in craniofacial tissues.
quotes: we located expression in craniofacial tissues

notes.statement: Losekoot et al. (2012) noted that renal cystic disease is generally milder in patients with PKD2 mutations than in patients with PKD1 mutations. They reported, for the first time, a patient homozygous for an incompletely penetrant PKD2 missense variant who had neonatal-onset disease.
quotes: Renal cystic disease is generally milder in PKD2 patients than in PKD1 patients.
This study reports for the first time a patient with neonatal onset of PKD homozygous for an incomplete penetrant PKD2 missense variant due to uniparental disomy.

notes.statement: Bataille et al. (2011) suggested a possible association between heterotaxia and PKD2 mutations. Their reasons were that Pkd2-null mouse and zebrafish models have laterality defects, and that all 3 probands with ADPKD and laterality defects had a pathogenic PKD2 mutation, although PKD2 mutations account for only 15% of ADPKD families. They recommended systematic screening for laterality defects in larger cohorts of ADPKD patients with PKD2 mutations.
quotes: A possible association between heterotaxia and a PKD2 mutation in our 3 patients is suggested by: (1) the existence of laterality defects in Pkd2-null mouse and zebrafish models and (2) detection of a pathogenic PKD2 mutation in the 3 probands, although PKD2 mutations account for only 15% of ADPKD families.
The presence of left-right laterality defects should be systematically screened in larger cohorts of patients with ADPKD harboring PKD2 mutations.

notes.statement: Pennekamp et al. (2002) generated a knockout allele of Pkd2 in mice. Along with malformations described previously, homozygous mutant embryos had right pulmonary isomerism and randomized embryonic turning, heart looping, and abdominal situs.
quotes: We have generated a knockout allele of Pkd2 in mouse. In addition to malformations described previously, homozygous mutant embryos showed right pulmonary isomerism, randomization of embryonic turning, heart looping, and abdominal situs.

notes.statement: In Pkd2-null mouse embryos, Pennekamp et al. (2002) found that Leftb and nodal were not expressed in the left lateral plate mesoderm and Ebaf was absent from the floorplate. Pitx2 was expressed on both sides in posterior LPM but was absent anteriorly. The embryonic midline was present and Foxa2 and shh were expressed at normal levels, which suggested that polycystin-2 acts downstream of or in parallel to shh and upstream of the nodal cascade.
quotes: Leftb and nodal were not expressed in the left lateral plate mesoderm (LPM), and Ebaf was absent from floorplate. Pitx2 was bilaterally expressed in posterior LPM but absent anteriorly.
The embryonic midline, however, was present, and normal levels of Foxa2 and shh were expressed, suggesting that polycystin-2 acts downstream or in parallel to shh and upstream of the nodal cascade.

notes.statement: Pennekamp et al. (2002) found that Pkd2 was expressed throughout mouse embryos at the headfold and early somite stages, with higher levels in the floorplate and notochord.
quotes: Pkd2 was ubiquitously expressed at headfold and early somite stages, with higher levels in floorplate and notochord.

notes.statement: Deltas (2001) reviewed the reported mutations in the PKD2 gene. Mutations of all kinds had been reported over the entire sequence of PKD2, with no apparent significant clustering and some evidence of genotype/phenotype correlation. Most families harbored their own private mutations, but a few recurrent mutations had been reported in unrelated families.
quotes: Mutations of all kinds have been reported over the entire sequence of the PKD2 gene, with no apparent significant clustering and with some evidence of genotype/phenotype correlation.
Most families harbor their own private mutations but a few recurrent events have been reported in unrelated families.

notes.statement: Deltas (2001) noted that PKD1 and PKD2 disease could not be told apart on clinical grounds, but patients with PKD2 mutations had a milder course. Their average age of onset was 10 to 20 years later, and they were less likely to reach end-stage renal failure.
quotes: The only difference is that patients with PKD2 mutations run a milder course compared to PKD1 carriers, with an average 10-20 years later age of onset and lower probability to reach end-stage-renal failure.

notes.statement: Deltas (2001) stated that renal cysts most probably arise after a second somatic event. This event inactivates the inherited healthy allele of the same gene, or perhaps an allele of the other polycystin gene, producing a trans-heterozygous state.
quotes: Renal cysts most probably arise after a second somatic event, which inactivates the inherited healthy allele of the same gene, or perhaps one of the alleles of the other gene counterpart, generating a trans-heterozygous state.

notes.statement: Pei et al. (2001) studied a large family (NFL10) previously excluded from linkage to both PKD1 and PKD2 and found bilineal disease: a PKD2 mutation (2152delA; L736X) in 12 affected members and, by linkage (LOD >3.0), a presumed PKD1 mutation in 15 other affected members lacking the PKD2 mutation.
quotes: Inspection of the haplotypes of these individuals suggested the possibility of bilineal disease from independently segregating PKD1 and PKD2 mutations.
These findings strongly support the presence of a PKD1 mutation in 15 other affected pedigree members, who lack the PKD2 mutation.

notes.statement: Pei et al. (2001) found that 2 individuals trans-heterozygous for PKD1 and PKD2 mutations had more severe renal disease than those with either mutation alone, indicating that trans-heterozygosity is not necessarily embryonically lethal in humans.
quotes: In humans, trans-heterozygous mutations involving both PKD1 and PKD2 are not necessarily embryonically lethal. However, the disease associated with the presence of both mutations appears to be more severe than the disease associated with either mutation alone.

notes.statement: Pei et al. (2001) cautioned that bilineal disease must be considered as a confounder in the search for a putative PKD3 locus.
quotes: The presence of bilineal disease as a confounder needs to be considered seriously in the search for the elusive PKD3 locus.

notes.statement: Watnick et al. (2000) found somatic mutations of PKD2 in 71% of renal cysts analyzed from patients with ADPKD2, supporting a two-hit mechanism of cyst formation.
quotes: Here we find somatic mutations of PKD2 in 71% of ADPKD2 cysts analysed.

notes.statement: Watnick et al. (2000) identified clonal somatic mutations of PKD1 in a subset of ADPKD2 cysts that lacked somatic PKD2 mutations, suggesting a pathogenic effect of trans-heterozygous mutations in PKD1 and PKD2, whose products associate to form heteromeric complexes.
quotes: Clonal somatic mutations of PKD1 were identified in a subset of cysts that lacked PKD2 mutations.
The products of these genes associate to form heteromeric complexes.

notes.statement: Koptides et al. (2000) studied DNA from cysts in the kidney of an ADPKD1 patient who carried a germline PKD1 mutation. Some cysts had somatic mutations in PKD1, and others had somatic mutations in PKD2. This created a trans-heterozygous state with mutations in both genes. The authors took this as the first direct genetic evidence that polycystins 1 and 2 interact, perhaps as part of a larger complex.
quotes: In cystic DNA from a kidney of an ADPKD1 patient, we showed somatic mutations not only in the PKD1 gene of certain cysts, but also in the PKD2 gene of others, generating a trans -heterozygous state with mutations in both genes.
One mutation in PKD1 is of germinal nature and the mutation in the PKD2 gene is of somatic nature.
Here, we provide the first direct genetic evidence that polycystins 1 and 2 do interact, perhaps as part of a larger complex.

notes.statement: Koptides et al. (2000) cited their own earlier finding that 9 of 23 cysts from a human ADPKD2 kidney had somatic mutations inactivating the inherited normal allele. They said this supported a two-hit loss-of-function model for ADPKD2 cystogenesis.
quotes: recently we showed that somatic mutations inactivating the inherited healthy allele were present in 9 of 23 cysts from a human ADPKD2 kidney, supporting a two-hit loss-of-function model for ADPKD2 cystogenesis.

notes.statement: Wu et al. (2000) made two mutations in mouse Pkd2. One was an unstable allele (WS25) that can undergo somatic rearrangement driven by homologous recombination to form a null allele. The other was a true null allele (WS183). Pkd2 -/- mice died in utero between embryonic day 13.5 and birth, with defects in cardiac septation and cysts in maturing nephrons and pancreatic ducts.
quotes: an unstable allele (WS25; hereafter denoted Pkd2WS25) that can undergo homologous-recombination-based somatic rearrangement to form a null allele; and a true null mutation (WS183; hereafter denoted Pkd2-)
Pkd2-/- mice die in utero between embryonic day (E) 13.5 and parturition. They have structural defects in cardiac septation and cyst formation in maturing nephrons and pancreatic ducts.

notes.statement: Wu et al. (2000) found that adult Pkd2 WS25/- mice developed kidney cysts, renal failure and early death (median survival 65 weeks vs 94 weeks in controls). These mice also had pancreatic ductal cysts. The authors suggested that cyst formation in ADPKD, including the pancreatic manifestation, occurs by a two-hit mechanism.
quotes: Pancreatic ductal cysts also occur in adult Pkd2WS25/- mice, suggesting that this clinical manifestation of ADPKD also occurs by a two-hit mechanism.
As in human ADPKD, formation of kidney cysts in adult Pkd2WS25/- mice is associated with renal failure and early death (median survival, 65 weeks versus 94 weeks for controls).

notes.statement: Wu et al. (2000) found that adult Pkd2 +/- mice had survival between that of controls and Pkd2 WS25/- mice, even though they had no cystic disease or renal failure. This was the first sign that Pkd2 haploinsufficiency harms long-term survival.
quotes: Adult Pkd2+/- mice have intermediate survival in the absence of cystic disease or renal failure, providing the first indication of a deleterious effect of haploinsufficiency at Pkd2on long-term survival.

notes.statement: Torra et al. (1999) studied 30 renal cysts from a PKD2 patient whose germline mutation was a deletion of most of the PKD2 gene. Loss of the wild-type allele was found in 10% of cysts, and SSCP screening of 6 exons found 8 different somatic mutations, all predicted to truncate the protein; overall at least 37% of cysts had somatic mutations.
quotes: Loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH) studies showed loss of the wild-type allele in 10% of cysts. Screening of six exons of the gene by SSCP detected eight different somatic mutations, all of them expected to produce truncated proteins.
Overall, >/=37% of the cysts studied presented somatic mutations.

notes.statement: Torra et al. (1999) found no loss of heterozygosity for PKD1 or locus D3S1478 in the cysts, showing that the somatic changes were specific to PKD2. They suggested that a second-hit mechanism could be a crucial event in cystogenesis in ADPKD type 2.
quotes: No LOH for the PKD1 gene or locus D3S1478 were observed in those cysts, which demonstrates that somatic alterations are specific.
We have identified second-hit mutations in human PKD2 cysts, which suggests that this mechanism could be a crucial event in the development of cystogenesis in human ADPKD-type 2.

notes.statement: Hateboer et al. (1999) compared 291 individuals with PKD2 from 31 families with 333 PKD1 patients and 398 controls. Median age at death or onset of end-stage renal disease was 69.1 years in PKD2, 53.0 years in PKD1, and 78.0 years in controls; age at presentation with kidney failure was later in PKD2 (median 74.0 vs 54.3 years).
quotes: Median age at death or onset of end-stage renal disease was 53.0 years (95% CI 51.2-54.8) in individuals with PKD1, 69.1 years (66.9-71.3) in those with PKD2, and 78.0 years (73.8-82.2) in controls.
Age at presentation with kidney failure was later in PKD2 than in PKD1 (median age 74.0 [67.2-80.8] vs 54.3 [52.7-55.9] years).

notes.statement: Hateboer et al. (1999) found that PKD2 patients were less likely than PKD1 patients to have hypertension (OR 0.25), a history of urinary tract infection (OR 0.50), or hematuria (OR 0.59). They concluded that although PKD2 is clinically milder than PKD1, it has a deleterious impact on life expectancy and cannot be regarded as benign.
quotes: PKD2 patients were less likely to have hypertension (odds ratio 0.25 [95% CI 0.15-0.42]), a history of urinary-tract infection (0.50 [0.31-0.83]), or haematuria (0.59 [0.35-0.98]).
Although PKD2 is clinically milder than PKD1, it has a deleterious impact on overall life expectancy and cannot be regarded as a benign disorder.

notes.statement: Hateboer et al. (1999) found that women with PKD2 had a significantly longer median survival than men (71.0 vs 67.3 years), whereas no sex influence was apparent in PKD1.
quotes: Women with PKD2 had a significantly longer median survival than men (71.0 [67.4-74.8] vs 67.3 [64.9-69.7] years), but no sex influence was apparent in PKD1.

notes.statement: Koptides et al. (1999) found somatic PKD2 mutations in renal cyst epithelial cells from both kidneys of an ADPKD2 patient: 7 of 21 cysts (33%) had the same C insertion in the inherited wild-type allele, and 2 others had a nonsense mutation or a splice site AG deletion. They suggested that ADPKD2 occurs by a cellular recessive mechanism, supporting a two-hit model for cyst formation.
quotes: From a total of 21 cysts examined, seven (33%) had the same C insertion within the inherited wild-type allele.
We suggest that the autosomal dominant form of ADPKD2 occurs by a cellular recessive mechanism, supporting a two-hit model for cyst formation.

notes.statement: Koptides et al. (1999) stated that PKD1 on chromosome 16 accounts for approximately 85% of ADPKD cases, PKD2 on chromosome 4 for approximately 15%, and PKD3 mutations are rare.
quotes: PKD1 on chromosome 16 accounts for approximately 85% of cases whereas PKD2 on chromosome 4 accounts for approximately 15%. Mutations in the PKD3 gene are rare.

notes.statement: Pei et al. (1998) used SSCP to screen all 15 exons of PKD2 in 11 Canadian ADPKD families. Four of the families had previously documented linkage to PKD2, and the other seven included members with ESRD at age 70 or older. They found mutations in 8 of the 11 families (about 73%), and the detection rate was the same in both groups. All the mutations lay between exons 1 and 11 and were predicted to produce a truncated polycystin-2 lacking the EF-hand domain and the cytoplasmic interaction domains. This suggested that most PKD2 mutations are inactivating.
quotes: A spectrum of mutations was found in approximately 73% (8 of 11) of the families screened, with no difference in the detection rate between the PKD2-linked families and the families with late-onset ESRD.

All mutations, scattered between exons 1 and 11, are predicted to result in a truncated polycystin 2 that lacks both the calcium-binding EF-hand domain and the two cytoplasmic domains required for the interaction of polycystin 2 with polycystin 1 and with itself.
suggest that most PKD2 mutations are inactivating

notes.statement: Pei et al. (1998) found insertion or deletion of an adenosine in a polyadenosine (A)8 tract at nucleotides 2152-2159 in exon 11 in 3 unrelated families. This suggested that this mononucleotide repeat is prone to mutation by slipped-strand mispairing.
quotes: In three unrelated families, insertion or deletion of an adenosine in a polyadenosine tract (i.e., (A)8 at nt 2152-2159) was found on exon 11, suggesting that this mononucleotide repeat tract is prone to mutations from "slipped strand mispairing."

notes.statement: Pei et al. (1998) found no correlation between where a mutation lay in the PKD2 coding sequence and disease severity.
quotes: Furthermore, no correlation was found between the location of the mutations in the PKD2 coding sequence and disease severity.

notes.statement: Wu et al. (1998) put a mutant exon 1 next to the wild-type exon 1 at the mouse Pkd2 locus. This created an unstable allele that becomes a true null through somatic intragenic homologous recombination. Mice heterozygous or homozygous for this allele, and Pkd2 +/- mice, developed polycystic kidney and liver lesions that could not be told apart from the human phenotype.
quotes: We have introduced a mutant exon 1 in tandem with the wild-type exon 1 at the mouse Pkd2 locus. This is an unstable allele that undergoes somatic inactivation by intragenic homologous recombination to produce a true null allele.
Mice heterozygous and homozygous for this mutation, as well as Pkd+/- mice, develop polycystic kidney and liver lesions that are indistinguishable from the human phenotype.

notes.statement: In the Pkd2 mouse models, Wu et al. (1998) found that renal cysts always arose from tubular cells that had lost the ability to make Pkd2 protein. They concluded that somatic loss of Pkd2 expression is both necessary and sufficient for renal cyst formation, suggesting that the disease arises by a cellular recessive mechanism.
quotes: In all cases, renal cysts arise from renal tubular cells that lose the capacity to produce Pkd2 protein.
Somatic loss of Pkd2 expression is both necessary and sufficient for renal cyst formation in ADPKD, suggesting that PKD2 occurs by a cellular recessive mechanism.

notes.statement: Viribay et al. (1997) screened all 15 exons of the PKD2 gene in chromosome 4-linked ADPKD families by heteroduplex and SSCP analyses and identified 7 novel mutations, a detection rate of approximately 90%. All mutations led to premature termination of translation (4 nonsense and 3 frameshifting deletions), were unique, and were distributed throughout the gene without clustering.
quotes: Here we report a systematic mutation screening of all 15 exons of the PKD2 gene in chromosome 4-linked ADPKD families, using heteroduplex and SSCP analyses.
All mutations are unique and are distributed throughout the gene without evidence of clustering.

notes.statement: Viribay et al. (1997) found no clear correlation between specific PKD2 mutations and the clinical profile in ADPKD2 families.
quotes: Comparison of specific mutations with the clinical profile in ADPKD2 families shows no clear correlation.

notes.statement: Veldhuisen et al. (1997) screened the PKD2 gene by SSCP analysis in 35 families with type 2 ADPKD and identified 20 mutations, most of which appeared unique and were distributed throughout the gene without clustering. They included small deletions, insertions, and substitutions leading to premature stops, 1 amino acid substitution, and 5 possible splice-site mutations.
quotes: We have systematically screened the gene for mutations by single-strand conformation-polymorphism analysis in 35 families with the second type of ADPKD and have identified 20 mutations.
So far, most mutations found seem to be unique and occur throughout the gene, without any evidence of clustering.

notes.statement: Veldhuisen et al. (1997) concluded that their findings suggest that the first step toward cyst formation in PKD2 patients is the loss of one functional copy of polycystin-2.
quotes: These findings suggest that the first step toward cyst formation in PKD2 patients is the loss of one functional copy of polycystin-2.

notes.statement: Mochizuki et al. (1996) identified a second gene for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, PKD2, by positional cloning.
quotes: A second gene for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease was identified by positional cloning.

notes.statement: Mochizuki et al. (1996) found that the predicted 968-amino acid PKD2 protein has 6 transmembrane spans with intracellular N and C termini, shows amino acid similarity to PKD1, its C. elegans homolog, and the family of voltage-activated calcium (and sodium) channels, and contains a potential calcium-binding domain.
quotes: The predicted 968-amino acid sequence of the PKD2 gene product has six transmembrane spans with intracellular amino- and carboxyl-termini.

The PKD2 protein has amino acid similarity with PKD1, the Caenorhabditis elegans homolog of PKD1, and the family of voltage-activated calcium (and sodium) channels, and it contains a potential calcium-binding domain.

notes.statement: Fossdal et al. (1993) did linkage analysis in 7 Icelandic families with ADPKD using markers flanking the PKD1 region on 16p13.3. The disease locus mapped to the PKD1 region in 4 families, but 3 families were unlinked to 16p13.3.
quotes: We have mainly used 3 highly polymorphic DNA markers, 3'HVR (D16S85), 16AC2.5 (D16S291) and SM7 (D16S283), flanking the PKD1 region on chromosome 16p13.3 to establish linkage status in seven Icelandic families with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
In four families, the disease locus is in the PKD1 region, and three families are "unlinked" to chromosome 16p13.3.

notes.statement: In 1 of the families unlinked to 16p13.3, Fossdal et al. (1993) excluded the disease locus from part of the long arm of chromosome 2. They suggested that more than 2 loci may be responsible for ADPKD. Their data also confirmed the location of the YNH24 (D2S44) locus on 2q13-q24.
quotes: In one of the "unlinked" families, the disease locus is excluded from a part of the long arm of chromosome 2, and we support a theory of more than 2 loci being responsible for ADPKD.
Our data confirm the location of the locus YNH24 (D2S44) to chromosome 2q13-q24.

notes.statement: Kimberling et al. (1993) typed over 100 microsatellite markers in the large Sicilian kindred in which genetic heterogeneity of ADPKD was first found. They mapped a second ADPKD gene to chromosome 4q13-q23, in a segment of about 9 cM flanked by D4S231 and D4S414.
quotes: This search has resulted in the successful localization of a second ADPKD gene to chromosome 4q.
It was found to be flanked by the markers D4S231 and D4S414, defining a segment that spans about 9 cM.

notes.statement: Kimberling et al. (1993) designated the new ADPKD locus on chromosome 4q as PKD4.
quotes: The new locus has been designated PKD4.

notes.statement: Kimberling et al. (1993) noted that at least two loci exist for ADPKD. One had been mapped to 16p, while the second, less common locus had remained unlinked until this study.
quotes: At least two loci are known to exist for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). One was localized to 16p, but the second less common locus has remained unlinked.

notes.statement: Kimberling et al. (1993) suggested that using flanking markers for both the second ADPKD gene and PKD1 would help identify the ADPKD subtype in a family. They expected this to make linkage-based presymptomatic diagnosis more accurate by reducing the error caused by genetic heterogeneity.
quotes: when flanking markers for the second ADPKD gene are used in conjunction with flanking markers for PKD1, the accuracy of the diagnosis of the subtype of ADPKD present in any particular family will be enhanced.
This will improve the accuracy of linkage-based presymptomatic diagnoses by reducing the error due to genetic heterogeneity.

notes.statement: Peters et al. (1993) used highly polymorphic microsatellite markers to assign a second ADPKD gene to chromosome 4. In 8 families with clear evidence against linkage to chromosome 16 markers, linkage analysis with markers D4S231 and D4S423 gave a multipoint lod score of 22.42.
quotes: Using highly polymorphic microsatellite DNA markers, we have assigned a second gene for ADPKD to chromosome 4.
In eight families with clear evidence against linkage to chromosome 16 markers, linkage analysis with the markers D4S231 and D4S423, demonstrated a multipoint lod score of 22.42.

notes.statement: Peters et al. (1993) noted that ADPKD is genetically heterogeneous: a gene defect on the short arm of chromosome 16 is responsible for the disease in roughly 86% of affected European families.
quotes: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder. A gene defect located on the short arm of chromosome 16 is responsible for the disease in roughly 86% of affected European families.

notes.statement: Jeffery et al. (1993) excluded linkage to the PKD1 region in a Sicilian family with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. For the flanking markers 3'HVR and SM7, the lod scores were -1.4 and -2.33, respectively, with theta max of 0.5 for each marker.
quotes: LOD scores for the polymorphic markers 3'HVR and SM7 flanking the PKD 1 locus, were -1.4 and -2.33 respectively, and theta max was 0.5 for each marker.

notes.statement: Jeffery et al. (1993) suggested that clinic populations may represent the most severe forms of the disease, while non-PKD1 disease is less aggressive. If so, genetic heterogeneity of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in the population may be much greater than currently suggested.
quotes: Assuming that a clinic population represents the most severe forms of a disease and non PKD-1 is a less aggressive phenotype, the degree of genetic heterogeneity for APKD in the population may well be much greater than at present suggested.

notes.statement: San Millán et al. (1995) confirmed linkage of ADPKD to chromosome 4q markers in 8 Spanish families not linked to 16p13.3, obtaining a maximum lod score of 9.03 at theta = 0.00 with marker D4S423. Multipoint analysis and recombinant haplotypes placed the PKD2 locus between D4S1542 and D4S1563, an interval of approximately 1 cM.
quotes: By linkage analysis with marker D4S423, a maximum lod score of 9.03 at a recombination fraction of .00 was obtained.
Multipoint linkage analysis, as well as a study of recombinant haplotypes, placed the PKD2 locus between D4S1542 and D4S1563, thereby defining a genetic interval of approximately 1 cM.

notes.statement: San Millán et al. (1995) noted that in about 86% of affected European families ADPKD was due to a gene defect at 16p13.3, with a second locus at 4q13-q23 accounting for the remaining families.
quotes: In approximately 86% of affected European families, a gene defect localized to 16p13.3 was responsible for ADPKD, while a second locus has been recently localized to 4q13-q23 as candidate for the disease in the remaining families.

notes.statement: Coto et al. (1995) studied 17 large Spanish families with ADPKD. Five of the families showed negative linkage to markers at 16p13.3 and significant linkage to the PKD2 locus on 4q. The authors concluded that mutations at only two loci cause the disease in most, if not all, of the families.
quotes: Five of the 17 families showed negative linkage for the 16p13.3 markers. In these families significant linkage to 4q was obtained.
mutations at only two loci are responsible for the development of the disease in most if not all the families

notes.statement: Coto et al. (1995) found that renal cysts developed at an earlier age in PKD1 mutation carriers. End-stage renal failure occurred at an older age in people with PKD2. Patients with ADPKD2 therefore had a better prognosis than those with PKD1 mutations.
quotes: Renal cysts developed at an earlier age in PKD1 mutation carriers, and end stage renal failure occurred at an older age in people affected with PKD2.
subjects with ADPKD2 having a better prognosis than those with mutations at PKD1

notes.statement: Romeo et al. (1988) found no linkage between the disease and the alpha-globin genes on 16p in an Italian family with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. They concluded that the condition can be caused by mutations in a second gene, and that the clinical features in this family could not be distinguished from those in the families linked to chromosome 16.
quotes: In an Italian family, absence of linkage between the disease mutation and alpha-globin indicates that the condition can be caused by mutations in a second gene.
The clinical features of the disease in this Italian family are indistinguishable from those found in the "linked" families.

notes.statement: Romeo et al. (1988) noted that because there are two polycystic kidney disease genes, linkage has to be shown separately in each family before predictive tests with DNA probes can be used reliably.
quotes: The finding that there are two polycystic kidney disease genes means that linkage must be demonstrated independently in each family before predictive tests with DNA probes can be used reliably.

notes.statement: Kimberling et al. (1988) studied a 5-generation kindred of Sicilian descent with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in which the disorder was not linked to the alpha-hemoglobin complex on 16p; the recombination frequency exceeded 24%, indicating a mutation at a different locus. They concluded that there is a second gene for ADPKD.
quotes: In this family the frequency of recombination between the alpha-hemoglobin complex and the region previously shown to contain the mutation causing polycystic kidney disease exceeded 24 percent, indicating a mutation at a different locus.
We conclude that there is a second gene for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

notes.statement: Kimberling et al. (1988) performed linkage studies with DNA probes on 163 members of the kindred, 71 of whom were affected by or at risk for ADPKD, and excluded linkage to the alpha-hemoglobin complex on chromosome 16p.
quotes: DNA probes were used in genetic-linkage studies on blood samples from 163 family members, of whom 71 were affected by or at risk for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

notes.statement: Kimberling et al. (1988) cautioned that, because of locus heterogeneity, prenatal and presymptomatic diagnosis of ADPKD by linkage must be approached with caution until the two forms can be distinguished.
quotes: This apparent heterogeneity means that prenatal and presymptomatic diagnosis must be approached with caution until a method is found to distinguish between the two forms of the disease.

notes.statement: Bachner et al. (1990) found no linkage to markers at the PKD1 locus on 16p in a large 3-generation family with autosomal dominant PKD with reduced penetrance. Lod scores with the 3'HVR marker ranged from 1.31 to -21.47 at theta = 0 depending on the model, and Smith's heterogeneity test gave a conditional probability of non-linkage between 0.9 and 1.0.
quotes: Results varied from Z = 1.31 to Z = -21.47 (theta = 0). Smith's test of heterogeneity gave a conditional probability of non-linkage between 0.9 and 1.0.
We conclude that this family presents a form of autosomal dominant PKD with reduced penetrance and no linkage to the PKD1 locus on the short arm of chromosome 16.

notes.statement: Bachner et al. (1990) also considered other explanations: 2 distinct hereditary diseases in the family, or a new mutation in one branch of the family together with a high frequency of isolated renal cysts.
quotes: Other hypotheses, such as the existence of two distinct hereditary diseases in this large family, or neomutation in one branch of the family associated with a high frequency of isolated renal cysts, are also considered.

notes.statement: Kumar et al. (1990) typed members of a large ADPKD family unlinked to chromosome 16 for 12 chromosome 1 markers. Multipoint analysis excluded ADPKD2 from the region between D1S81 and D1S67 on the long arm and between Rh and PGM1 on the short arm, which excluded the locus from about 61% of chromosome 1.
quotes: Multipoint analysis excluded ADPKD2 from the region between D1S81 (pTHH33) and D1S67 (pHHH106) on the long arm and between Rh and PGM1 on the short arm. This excludes the disease locus from about 61% of chromosome 1.

notes.statement: Kumar et al. (1990) pointed out that ADPKD shows genetic heterogeneity, because some families show linkage to markers on chromosome 16p and others do not.
quotes: recent studies have shown genetic heterogeneity, with some, but not all, families showing linkage with markers on chromosome 16p.

notes.statement: Elles et al. (1990) typed 24 families with adult-onset polycystic kidney disease for markers flanking the PKD1 locus on chromosome 16. The aggregated results gave a significant lod score in favor of linkage to PKD1.
quotes: Twenty-four families with adult onset polycystic kidney disease were typed for markers flanking the PKD1 locus on chromosome 16. The aggregated results gave a significant lod score in favour of linkage to PKD1.

notes.statement: Elles et al. (1990) found 2 families that showed unusual features: recombinations with flanking markers, including double recombinations, and in one family an unexpectedly high proportion of affected people. They considered whether the disease in these families might be caused by a mutation at a second locus, PKD2, not linked to PKD1. Comparing apparently nonrecombinant with doubly recombinant meioses, they concluded that neither their families nor previously published data gave compelling evidence for a second locus.
quotes: Within this group of families two showed unusual features: recombinations, including double recombinations, and, in one family, an unexpectedly high proportion of affected people.
We consider the evidence that in these families the disease might result from a mutation at a different locus, PKD2, not linked to PKD1.
Using this test, neither our two families nor the data published so far on other families provide compelling evidence for the existence of a second locus for adult polycystic kidney disease.

notes.statement: Elles et al. (1990) proposed testing for a second locus by comparing the relative numbers of meioses that appear nonrecombinant and doubly recombinant for markers flanking the disease locus, ignoring meioses recombinant for only one marker. For genetic counseling in families too small to show evidence for or against linkage, they suggested handling the extra uncertainty by using a higher recombination rate.
quotes: We suggest that a useful test is to compare the relative numbers of meioses apparently non-recombinant and doubly recombinant for markers flanking the normal disease locus, ignoring meioses recombinant for only a single marker.
For genetic counselling in families too small to give internal evidence for or against linkage, the extra uncertainty can be handled by using a higher recombination rate.

notes.statement: Nørby and Schwartz (1990) proposed a possible locus for polycystic kidney disease on chromosome 2.
quotes: Possible locus for polycystic kidney disease on chromosome 2.

notes.statement: Kumar et al. (1991) studied a large Sicilian kindred with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, unlinked to chromosome 16, with over 250 members. Analysis of 29 informative marker loci on 11 autosomes significantly excluded linkage of the disease locus from 17 marker loci and showed no evidence of close linkage with the others.
quotes: A large PKD kindred, unlinked to chromosome 16, with over 250 members was studied using both DNA and classical markers.

In total, 29 informative marker loci on 11 autosomes have been analyzed for linkage with PKD. The data significantly exclude the linkage with disease locus from 17 marker loci and show no evidence of close linkage with the other loci.

notes.statement: Kumar et al. (1991) noted that polycystic kidney disease is caused by mutation in at least two different gene loci, with PKD1 on chromosome 16p and the location of a second locus unknown.
quotes: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is a common autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutation in at least two different gene loci.
The location of a second genetic locus in the human genome is not yet known.

notes.statement: Bear et al. (1992) found that the mean age of onset of ESRD was 68.7 years in affected members of 2 Newfoundland ADPKD families in which the disease was not co-inherited with PKD1 markers, compared with 56.3 years in persons with the PKD1 form (P = 0.01).
quotes: The mean (SE) age of onset of ESRD is 56.3 (1.8) years for persons with the PKD1 form of ADPKD, and 68.7 (1.7) years for affected members of families in which ADPKD is not co-inherited with PKD1 markers (P = 0.01).

notes.statement: Bear et al. (1992) reported that in 2 families with non-PKD1 ADPKD only 11% of members younger than 30 years had kidney cysts, whereas in PKD1-linked families the false-negative ultrasonographic diagnosis rate was estimated at 36% below age 10 and 8% or less thereafter.
quotes: In 2 families in which ADPKD is not co-inherited with PKD1 markers, only 11% of members aged less than 30 years had kidney cysts.
rates of false negative ultrasonographic diagnosis are estimated as 36% below the age of 10 years and 8% or less thereafter

notes.statement: Bear et al. (1992) found that of 17 Newfoundland ADPKD families, 10 showed linkage to PKD1 markers while in 2 families the disease was not co-inherited with PKD1 markers.
quotes: In 10 families showing genetic linkage between ADPKD and markers for the PKD1 locus
In 2 families in which ADPKD is not co-inherited with PKD1 markers

notes.statement: Ravine et al. (1992) compared 5 non-PKD1 ADPKD families (49 affected) with 18 PKD1-linked families (285 affected). Non-PKD1 patients lived longer (median survival 71.5 vs 56.0 years). They also had a lower risk of renal failure (odds ratio 0.35) and of hypertension (adjusted odds ratio 0.29), and were diagnosed later (median 69.1 vs 44.8 years) with fewer renal cysts at diagnosis.
quotes: Non-PKD1 patients lived longer than PKD1 patients (median survival 71.5 vs 56.0 years), had a lower risk of progressing to renal failure (odds ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.13-0.92), were less likely to have hypertension (odds ratio adjusted for age and family of origin 0.29, 0.11-0.80)

notes.statement: Ravine et al. (1992) identified 5 ADPKD families in which linkage to the PKD1 locus on chromosome 16 could be excluded. This supported locus heterogeneity in ADPKD.
quotes: It is now clear that mutations of at least two genetic loci can lead to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
5 families (49 affected individuals) in which involvement of this locus could be dismissed.

notes.statement: Ravine et al. (1992) noted that no non-PKD1 family was ascertained through renal impairment clinics. They concluded that, partly because of its milder phenotype, the reported prevalence of non-PKD1 ADPKD is probably an underestimate.
quotes: Although most of the PKD1 families were ascertained through clinics treating patients with renal impairment, no non-PKD1 family was identified through this source.
Partly as a result of this difference in severity, the reported prevalence of this genotype is probably an underestimate.
